title: Full-Text Search
description: Build full-text indexes and query them with CONTAINS, FREETEXT, and CONTAINSTABLE for linguistic search.

data.text: `LIKE '%keyboard%'` cannot use an index and degrades as the table grows. Full-text search builds a separate index of words and their positions, maintained by the full-text engine. It understands word boundaries, inflections, and stop words, and it can rank results by relevance. SQL Server has shipped full-text search since SQL Server 2000; the modern implementation uses the `sys.fulltext_*` catalog views and asynchronous population.

A full-text index needs a unique, single-column, non-nullable key index on the table. `CHANGE_TRACKING AUTO` keeps the full-text index in sync as rows change; `MANUAL` requires you to call `ALTER FULLTEXT INDEX ... START UPDATE POPULATION` after changes.

data.title: Create a full-text catalog and index
data.content: The language identifier 1033 is US English; it selects the word breaker and stoplist used to tokenize the text.
data.code:
CREATE FULLTEXT CATALOG ProductCatalog AS DEFAULT;
GO

CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX ON dbo.Products
(
    Name        LANGUAGE 1033,
    Description LANGUAGE 1033
)
KEY INDEX PK_Products
ON ProductCatalog
WITH CHANGE_TRACKING AUTO;
GO

data.text: `CONTAINS` is precise: it matches exact words, prefixes, inflections, and proximity. `FREETEXT` is looser: it splits the search string into words and matches any of them, including inflectional forms, so it behaves more like a search box than a query language.

data.title: CONTAINS with NEAR and FORMSOF
data.content: This finds products where 'wireless' and 'keyboard' appear within five words of each other, and products whose text contains an inflection of 'keyboard'.
data.code:
SELECT ProductId, Name, Description
FROM dbo.Products
WHERE CONTAINS((Name, Description), 'NEAR((wireless, keyboard), 5)')
   OR CONTAINS((Name, Description), 'FORMSOF(INFLECTIONAL, keyboard)');

data.title: Rank results with CONTAINSTABLE
data.content: CONTAINSTABLE returns a KEY column and a RANK column, so you can join back to the table and order by relevance.
data.code:
SELECT
    p.ProductId,
    p.Name,
    ft.RANK
FROM dbo.Products AS p
JOIN CONTAINSTABLE(
        dbo.Products,
        (Name, Description),
        'FORMSOF(INFLECTIONAL, keyboard)'
     ) AS ft
    ON ft.[KEY] = p.ProductId
ORDER BY ft.RANK DESC;

rows: Small tables or exact substring requirements
Word/phrase, prefix, inflection, proximity, weighted terms
Splits input into words and matches any inflection
You want a simple search box
You need to order results by relevance

data.title: Population is asynchronous
data.text: A newly created full-text index does not contain rows immediately. The population runs in the background, so test queries right after creation may return nothing. Check `sys.fulltext_indexes` and the full-text crawl logs. Stop words and the chosen language change results in ways that surprise people — test with real data.

data.title: Interview angle: full-text vs LIKE vs a search engine
data.text: Full-text search is a good fit when the corpus lives in SQL Server and you need word-based matching with ranking on a single table. It is not a replacement for Elasticsearch or Azure AI Search when you need faceting, fuzzy matching, cross-entity relevance, or horizontal scale. The honest answer is that SQL Server full-text handles modest search needs well and becomes awkward at search-engine scale.

data.title: Full-Text Search Key Points
points: Full-text search indexes words and positions, unlike LIKE which scans substrings.
Create a full-text catalog, then a full-text index with a unique key index.
CHANGE_TRACKING AUTO keeps the index current; MANUAL requires explicit population.
CONTAINS is precise; FREETEXT is looser; CONTAINSTABLE adds relevance ranking.
Population is asynchronous, so results lag behind writes.
Use a dedicated search engine when you need faceting, fuzzy matching, or horizontal scale.
